title: Why generics exist (type safety versus ArrayList boxing)
hook: Before generics, collections stored everything as object. That meant boxing value types, risky casts, and bugs that only showed up at run time. Generics let you write List<int> and have the compiler reject mistakes before your app ships.

blocks.text: Generics let you write code that works with many types while keeping each type separate at compile time. Instead of a bag of object, you declare a type parameter T — for example List<T> — and the compiler tracks whether you are working with int, string, or SessionDto. The Common Language Runtime (CLR) still knows the real type at run time, unlike TypeScript where generic parameters disappear after compilation.

entries.plainDefinition: Wrapping a value type (like int) inside a heap-allocated object so it can be stored where object is expected.
entries.example: ArrayList.Add(42) boxes the int into an object on the heap.

entries.plainDefinition: Keeping generic type information at run time. List<int> and List<string> are different types in the CLR.
entries.example: typeof(List<int>) is not the same as typeof(List<string>).

entries.plainDefinition: Removing generic type parameters before run time. Java and TypeScript erase; C# does not.
entries.example: A TypeScript function identity<T>(x: T) has no T left in the emitted JavaScript.

blocks.text: System.Collections.ArrayList and Hashtable stored object. Every int you added was boxed onto the heap. Reading back required a cast that could throw InvalidCastException if someone mixed types. In production code — message queues, caches, API payloads — that failure mode is unacceptable. List<T>, Dictionary<TKey, TValue>, and HashSet<T> are the everyday replacements: compile-time checks, no boxing for value types, and clearer intent.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: ArrayList = object + boxing + casts. List<T> = compile-time type checking, no boxing for structs, and a constructed type the CLR still knows at run time.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: From untyped collection to generic safety

items.title: Legacy collections accept object
items.body: ArrayList.Add(object) takes any value. Value types are boxed; reference types are stored as-is.

items.title: Reader must cast
items.body: Getting an element back returns object. You cast to int or string — and hope nobody changed the order.

items.title: Generics parameterize the type
items.body: List<int> only accepts int. The compiler rejects list.Add("oops") before you run the app.

items.title: CLR keeps the closed type
items.body: List<int> and List<string> are different constructed types. Reflection and the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler use that information.

diagram.title: ArrayList versus List<T>

flowchart LR

snippet.label: The cast that should never ship
snippet.explanation: List<int> stores ints directly in its backing array. ArrayList stored boxed objects. The compiler catches the mixed-type bug on List<T>; ArrayList only fails at run time with InvalidCastException.

snippet.label: Reification at run time
snippet.explanation: C# generics are reified: the CLR knows List<int> is not List<string>. TypeScript generics erase completely, so there is no typeof equivalent for T at run time.

snippet.label: Everyday generic collections
snippet.explanation: Production code reaches for BCL generic types daily. You write your own generic types when the invariant is yours — a cache client, a Result<T>, or a handler pipeline.

blocks.title: Generics: C# versus TypeScript
rows: Reified — List<int> is a real type
Erased — only exists for the compiler
All numbers are one JavaScript number type

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using List<object> as a quiet ArrayList — you lose type safety again. Saying C# generics work like C++ templates — C# does not generate a new source file per T; the JIT or Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compiler specializes at run time or publish time. Boxing anyway by storing structs as interface types inside a List<IComparable> when you meant List<int>.

blocks.text: C# generics are **reified**: `List<int>` and `List<string>` are distinct constructed types in CLR metadata — unlike Java or TypeScript erasure. At the native-code level, the runtime uses **generic sharing** for reference-type type arguments: `List<string>` and `List<object>` (when legal) often share one JIT-compiled body because reference types share the same representation size; value-type arguments get specialized native code per closed type (List<int> versus List<double>). That is why boxing in legacy ArrayList hurt both allocation and cache locality. How to prove it in production: `typeof(List<int>) != typeof(List<string>)` in a diagnostic endpoint; dotnet-counters GC allocation rate comparing ArrayList.Add loop versus List<int> on a hot SQS batch path.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Cast at read; mixed types at run time
One JIT body for reference T
Value types still specialize per T

snippet.label: Generic sharing — reference types vs value types
snippet.explanation: Reification gives you distinct types for reflection and casts. Generic sharing is an optimization: reference-type arguments reuse code; value types do not participate in IEnumerable<object> covariance.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying C# generics erase like Java — they do not; typeof(List<int>) works. Claiming List<object> is as safe as List<string> — it is a typed object bag that boxes ints again. Confusing C# generics with C++ template expansion — C# shares JIT code for reference type parameters. Strong answer: reified types, no boxing in List<int>, generic sharing for reference T args, prefer System.Collections.Generic.

interviewTakeaways: Generics give compile-time type safety and avoid boxing value types in collections.
C# generics are reified at run time; Java and TypeScript generics are erased.
Generic sharing: reference-type type arguments often share one JIT body; value types specialize per closed type.

60s: ArrayList boxed object and required casts. List<T> is reified, type-safe, no box for structs. typeof(List<int>) works. Reference-type T args share JIT code; value types get separate specializations.
Follow-up: why does IEnumerable<int> not convert to IEnumerable<object>?
commonPitfalls: Saying C# generics erase at run time like Java — that answer gets rejected; typeof(List<int>) proves reification.
Strong answer: reified constructed types; List<int> stores ints directly without boxing.
Using List<object> as a quiet ArrayList — you lose compile-time safety and box value types again.
Saying C# generates separate C++-style source per T — JIT/AOT specializes; reference types share code.

jsTsCorrelations.note: function identity<T>(x: T): T erases T before run time. C# identity<T> remains in metadata and can be invoked via reflection with a closed type argument.
JavaScript arrays accept any value — they behave like ArrayList. TypeScript only adds T as a compile-time annotation on top.
